newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi trial nurses gain time for new evidence.
newsitem.headline: Saudi trial nurses gain time for new evidence.

text.p: Defence lawyers of two British nurses on trial for murder in Saudi Arabia have been given two weeks to provide critical evidence that could save the nurses from the death sentence.
The trial, which resumed at Khobar sharia court on Sunday, adjourned after one hour. Sources close to the case said the trial would resume on August 10.

The Law firm Salah al-Hujailan, representing Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan 31, said the court was now leaning towards disqualifying the family of the Australian victim Yvonne Gilford from any role in determining the fate of the two nurses. Gilford's brother, Frank, has demanded the death penalty for the two accused.
Parry and McLauchlan are accused of murdering Yvonne Gilford, an Australian colleague, at the King Fahd military medical complex where all three worked.
Gilford, 55, was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the medical complex in the nearby oil city of Dhahran.

The court had initially questioned whether the power of attorney granted by the victim's mother Muriel Gilford, 84, to her son was valid. Muriel suffers from Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home in Australia.
The power of attorney gives Frank Gilford, the victim's brother, the right to speak on behalf of the victim's closest family -- made up of their mother and himself.
The Sharia court ruled earlier that Frank Gilford could speak for the family, giving him the right to demand execution if the alleged killers of his sister were found guilty.
"The court has demanded that within two weeks we will bring evidence of the mental condition of the (victim's) mother," a statement by al-Hujailan said.
"Upon the demonstration of the mental condition of the mother the court will most probably demand a guardian to be appointed by the Australian court," the statement said.
"Frank Gilford will not be considered in this situation to become the guardian," it added.

Convicted murderers in Saudi Arabia are usually beheaded by the sword in a public square. At least 72 people have been executed in the conservative Islamic kingdom this year for charges including murder.
Parry and McLauchlan have withdrawn confessions which they said they were forced into making. Both say they are innocent.

McLauchlan's parents and Parry's sister and brother-in-law are in Saudi Arabia and visited the two women over the weekend. It was not immediately known if the family members had attended Sunday's session.
